text: A decision tree makes predictions the way a checklist does — ask a yes-or-no question about one feature, follow the branch, ask another, and repeat until you reach an answer. Unlike the linear models of the last chapter, a tree doesn't fit one global formula — it carves the data into regions, one question at a time, and each region gets its own prediction.

Training is a greedy, recursive process. Look at every feature and every possible split point. Pick the split that makes the two resulting groups as pure as possible, meaning dominated by a single class. Repeat inside each new group until a stopping rule is hit. Each final group, a leaf, predicts the most common class among its training rows.

Purity is measured by Gini impurity — 0 for a perfectly pure group, growing as classes mix. A root node with 396 stayers and 164 churners has a Gini of about 0.414. A good split lowers the weighted impurity of the children.

Simulating 800 customers where new customers, heavy support users, and high-bill customers churn more: fitting a tree limited to depth 3 gives training accuracy 78.8 percent and test accuracy 78.3 percent. Always compare against a baseline — always predicting stay scores only 62.9 percent on this test set, so the tree adds real signal.

Plotting the tree shows each box's question, Gini score, row count, and majority class. The root splits on tenure less than or equal to 11.5 — the single most useful first question. Following a new customer with 6 months tenure, 1 support call, and a $95 monthly charge down the branches lands on a leaf predicting churn — a fully traceable path, the tree's greatest strength.

By default, a tree keeps splitting until every leaf is pure, which memorizes the training set. An unrestricted tree scores a perfect 1.0 on training data, using 18 levels and 156 leaves — but only 0.712 on test, worse than the small tree's 0.783. That's overfitting from Chapter 1, in a very direct form.

The knobs that control it are max_depth, min_samples_leaf, and min_samples_split, and you choose them with cross-validation, exactly as you learned for regularization. Strengths: trees are highly interpretable, handle numeric and encoded categorical features with no scaling needed, and capture non-linear effects automatically.

Weaknesses: prone to overfitting unless constrained, unstable — a small change in the data can produce a very different tree — and predictions are step-like rather than smooth. That instability is exactly the motivation for the next lesson: combine many trees so their individual errors cancel out. Next: random forests.
